blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: A flute is a long tube with holes in it. You do not bite it. You blow across a hole at the top. The air wiggles inside the tube. That wiggle is the sound. Cover a hole with your finger and the sound goes low. Lift your finger and the sound goes high. Blow soft and it sings soft. Blow hard and it sings loud.

blocks.prompt: The Tube Full of Air
blocks.text: A flute is a tube full of air. When you blow across the hole, the air inside the tube shakes very fast. Shaking air is what your ears hear. A short tube makes a high sound. A long tube makes a low sound. The holes let you change the length. When you cover the holes, the air has a long way to travel and the note is low. When you lift your fingers, the air gets out sooner and the note is high. People made flutes out of bone and wood a long time before anyone made one out of metal.

blocks.prompt: The Oldest Instrument We Have Found
blocks.text: In a cave in Germany called Hohle Fels, diggers found a thin tube of bone with finger holes cut into it. It was made from the wing bone of a big bird called a griffon vulture. It is about 40,000 years old. That makes it the oldest musical instrument anyone has ever found. People were making music before they were farming, before they were writing, before they had metal tools of any kind. A flute is simple, and that is why it is old. It has no strings and no reed. You blow a thin ribbon of air across the sharp edge of a hole. The air splits at the edge and starts flipping back and forth very fast. That flipping makes the air inside the tube shake, and shaking air is sound. Covering and uncovering the holes changes how long the shaking column of air is. Long column, low note. Short column, high note. Somebody worked all of that out with a bone and a stone tool, a very long time ago.

blocks.prompt: How a Tube Makes a Note
blocks.text: A flute makes sound in a way that seems like cheating, because nothing on the instrument is designed to vibrate. A violin has strings. A clarinet has a thin reed that flaps. A flute has neither. What vibrates is the air itself. The player aims a narrow ribbon of breath across the sharp far edge of the mouth hole. That edge splits the ribbon. Part of the air is pushed into the tube, part slips over the top, and the stream flips between the two sides hundreds of times every second. Musicians call this an edge tone. The flipping stream pumps the column of air inside the tube, and that column vibrates as a whole. Your ear reads the vibration as a note. The pitch depends almost entirely on the length of the vibrating column. Open a hole partway down the tube and the column effectively ends there, so it is shorter and the note is higher. Close all the holes and the column runs the full length of the instrument, giving the lowest note the flute can play. A concert flute is roughly 26 inches long and its bottom note is middle C. A piccolo is half that length and sings an octave higher. There is one more trick. If the player narrows the airstream and blows faster, the same fingering suddenly leaps up an octave. The column splits into two halves that vibrate separately. That is why a flute with only a handful of holes can still cover a wide range of notes. Beginners spend weeks learning to make any sound at all, because the ribbon of air has to be aimed with real precision. Most of the breath never goes into the flute. It spills over the edge and disappears into the room.

blocks.prompt: The Instrument Everyone Invented
blocks.text: Almost every human culture invented the flute, separately, without borrowing the idea from anyone. India has the bansuri, a length of bamboo with six or seven holes. China has the dizi, which carries a thin paper membrane stretched over an extra hole so the tone buzzes and carries. Japan has the shakuhachi, blown across the rim at the end of the tube rather than the side. The Andes have the quena, the Middle East has the ney, and Europe eventually produced the silver concert flute. The reason for that independence is simple. A flute is the least demanding instrument to build. You need a hollow tube and a sharp edge. Bamboo, bone, cane, and clay all supply one. For most of that history the flute had a problem that no maker could solve. Holes have to sit where the physics of the vibrating air column wants them, but fingers can only stretch so far. Makers compromised. They drilled holes where hands could reach, which put several notes slightly out of tune, and players learned to correct those notes by rolling the instrument or half covering a hole. Every flutist simply accepted that some notes were harder to play in tune than others. In the 1830s a German flutist and goldsmith named Theobald Boehm decided the compromise was backwards. He placed the holes exactly where the acoustics demanded, made them as large as the tone wanted, and then engineered a system of padded keys, rods, and springs so that ordinary human fingers could still close them. He also replaced the cone shaped wooden body with a cylindrical metal tube, which evened out the tone across the range. Older players complained that the new flute sounded cold. They lost the argument. The Boehm flute of 1847 is very nearly the flute in orchestras today, which is why a modern flute is metal and yet is still counted as a woodwind. The family name describes how the sound is made, not what the tube is made of.

blocks.prompt: Forty Thousand Years of Blowing Across a Hole
blocks.text: The oldest musical instrument yet found is a flute, and it is not close. In the Hohle Fels cave in southern Germany, archaeologists recovered a slim tube cut from the wing bone of a griffon vulture, drilled with finger holes and notched at one end where the player's breath would strike. It is roughly 40,000 years old. Nearby sites have produced flutes carved from mammoth ivory, which is a far harder project: the maker had to split the tusk lengthwise, hollow out both halves, and seal them back together airtight. Nobody does that by accident. Someone wanted a particular sound badly enough to spend days getting it. Music, on this evidence, is older than agriculture, older than writing, older than metal. The reason the flute got there first is that it asks the least of its maker. Consider what other instruments require. A drum needs a hide, prepared and stretched and kept tensioned. A string instrument needs gut or sinew twisted to an even thickness and held under tension by a frame that will not warp. A reed instrument needs a slip of cane shaved thin enough to flex thousands of times a second without splitting. A flute needs a tube and a sharp edge. Bamboo grows as a tube. A leg bone is already a tube. The engineering was mostly done by nature. What happens inside that tube is genuinely strange, and it is worth being precise about. No part of a flute vibrates. The player directs a narrow ribbon of air across the far edge of the mouth hole, and the edge splits the ribbon so that it flips in and out of the tube hundreds of times a second, producing what acousticians call an edge tone. That oscillation drives the column of air inside the tube, and the column resonates as a single body. The note you hear is the frequency of that resonance, and it is set by the length of the column. Uncover a hole and you shorten the column, raising the pitch. Cover everything and the column runs the full length of the bore, giving the lowest available note. Blow faster and narrower and the column divides into two vibrating halves, jumping the pitch a full octave without moving a finger. For most of human history, flute makers fought a losing battle between physics and anatomy. Acoustics dictates where a tone hole belongs and how wide it should be. Hands dictate where a finger can reach. Makers sided with the hands, drilled the holes where fingers fell, and accepted that certain notes would sit slightly out of tune. Players learned private corrections for those notes and taught them to their students as craft knowledge. In the 1830s Theobald Boehm, a German flutist who was also a trained goldsmith, refused the trade. He sited each hole where the acoustics demanded, sized each hole as the tone required, and then built an apparatus of rods, axles, springs, and padded keys so that human fingers could still seal holes they could not physically cover. He also replaced the tapering wooden body with a cylindrical metal one. Traditionalists said the result sounded thin and mechanical. They were overruled by every professional who wanted to play in tune. The flute in an orchestra tonight is essentially Boehm's 1847 design, which is why the instrument is metal and is still filed under woodwinds. The label describes the mechanism, not the material. The line from the vulture bone to the silver keywork is unbroken, and the physics never changed once.
